title: The $400 Million Machine Behind Every AI Chip
hook: Every AI chip starts on a machine most people have never heard of: a $400-million, bus-sized contraption from a single Dutch company that the whole industry depends on.
key_points: MIT Technology Review profiles ASML's newest chipmaking machine — around $400 million each.
It's the size of a double-decker bus: 150+ tons of precision aluminum, tubes, cables, and tanks.
Machines like these print the microscopic circuitry that makes modern chips — including AI chips — possible.
ASML, one Dutch company, dominates the market for the most advanced of these machines.
That concentration makes the machine a strategic chokepoint for the whole AI hardware supply chain.
content_html: The AI boom is usually told as a software story, but it rests on an almost unbelievable piece of hardware. MIT Technology Review takes readers inside ASML's newest chipmaking machine — a contraption the size of a double-decker bus, more than 150 tons of precision-milled aluminum wrapped in thousands of tubes, cables, and pressurized tanks, with a price tag around $400 million.
extra_html: What these machines do is print the unimaginably tiny circuitry onto silicon — the patterns, far thinner than a human hair, that make a modern chip work. Without them, today's most advanced processors, including the ones training and running AI, simply couldn't be built. Here's the part worth remembering: ASML, a single Dutch company, dominates the market for the most advanced of these machines, and only a handful of factories worldwide can use them. That makes this one device a strategic chokepoint — which is exactly why chipmaking has become a flashpoint in global politics and trade. For a general reader, it's a vivid reminder that "AI" isn't just code in the cloud; it depends on a fragile, concentrated, jaw-droppingly complex physical supply chain that very few players control.

related.title: Who Controls AI?
related.hook: The most powerful AI models are built by a handful of giant companies, because training them costs a fortune. Who holds that power — and whether 'open' AI can balance it — shapes everything.
